newsitem.title: CANADA: Alcan settles Canadian lawsuit, mulls new smelter.
newsitem.headline: Alcan settles Canadian lawsuit, mulls new smelter.

text.p: Alcan Aluminium Ltd. on Tuesday settled a lawsuit against the British Columbia provincial government over its canceled Kemano hydroelectric project and said it might build a new C$1.2 billion ($876 million) smelter at Kitimat, British Columbia.

Montreal-based Alcan, the world's second largest aluminum producer, said that subject to economic and market conditions, the new 225,000 metric ton smelter could be operational as early as Jan. 1, 2003 and no later than Jan. 1, 2010.
Under the settlement, Alcan agreed to restart 22,000 metric tons of idle capacity at its existing 272,000-metric-ton Kitimat smelter and bring it to full capacity by Jan. 1, 1998.

Alcan said the agreement signals the end of a bitter court action, in which it sought damages for losses incurred at its half-completed Kemano Completion Project, canceled by the provincial government in January 1995.

Kitimat, in remote northwestern British Columbia near the Alaska border, is the site of Alcan's biggest smelter dating from the 1950s. Hoping to expand that smelter, Alcan began building a C$1.3 billion ($936 million) generating facility called Kemano in 1988 to provide more power to Kitimat.
But the Kemano project, which would have entailed diversion of the salmon-rich Nechako River, became mired in controversy amid allegations it would cause environmental damage and hurt fish stocks.
Alcan suspended the project in 1991. British Columbia convened a long public review and announced in 1995 it was forcing cancelation of the project.
Afterward, Alcan wrote off its $420 million investment in Kemano and sued the British Columbia government.
The settlement provides for a power replacement option that will allow Alcan to expand its British Columbia operations, while maintaining the company's power sales agreement with B.C. Hydro.

At a signing ceremony in Vancouver, British Columbia Premier Glen Clark said the province would provide Alcan with the 175 average annual megawatts of hydroelectric power it needs to expand its Kitimat smelter at the same rates the company would have had with its Kemano project.
Alcan Chief Executive Jacques Bougie said a final decision on the new Kitimat smelter could be made by the end of 1999, with construction beginning in 2000 or 2002.

Bougie said Alcan was "poised for growth...particularly in aluminum smelting," and that the Kitimat project would not affect a decision expected this year or early next year on a C$1.4 billion ($1 billion) 340,000-metric-ton expansion of the company's facilities in Alma, Quebec.

Bougie said world demand for aluminum was rising fast enough for both the Kitimat and Alma projects to go ahead. The Alma project would replace some of the company's older existing smelting capacity in Quebec.

While the proposed new smelter's capacity would probably be absorbed by the market by 2003 -- the earliest possible start-up time -- some metals analysts questioned whether the focus on smelting capacity was the right move.

"By 2003, a new smelter would probably be needed," said Thomas McNamara, an analyst at Oppenheimer & Co. "What I would like to have seen was a focus on where their weakness is, which is raw materials. They have a lot to do on that side of the market."
